analysis.evidence: Melchizedek pronounces God Most High (אֵל עֶלְיוֹן) blessed. The following clause gives the reason for his praise: God delivered Abram’s enemies into his hand.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וּ means “and.” The Qal passive participle בָרוּךְ is masculine singular absolute and serves as the predicate of אֵל עֶלְיוֹן.
analysis.sense: to pronounce Yahweh blessed in praise

analysis.evidence: וּבָרוּךְ אֵל עֶלְיוֹן means “and blessed be God Most High.” The following clause identifies him as the one who delivered Abram’s enemies into his hand.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix. The adjective עֶלְיוֹן modifies it.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 69139:5, 69138:10.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute adjective modifying אֵל, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces a relative clause describing אֵל עֶלְיוֹן, “God Most High,” as the one who delivered the enemies into Abram’s hand.

In the clause introduced by אֲשֶׁר, אֵל עֶלְיוֹן is the subject of מִגֵּן. The object צָרֶיךָ means “your enemies,” and בְּיָדֶךָ means “into your hand.” Melchizedek blesses God Most High for handing Abram’s enemies over to him.
analysis.morphology: Piel perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן צָרֶיךָ בְּיָדֶךָ, God Most High delivered Abram’s enemies into his hand. The noun names the foes Abram defeated, and the suffix identifies them as his enemies.
analysis.morphology: Masculine plural construct noun with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Abram.

analysis.evidence: לוֹ identifies the recipient (“to him”), and מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל identifies what he gave (“a tenth of everything”).
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ introduces a Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, continuing the narrative.
analysis.sense: give something to someone for their use

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּתֶּן לוֹ מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל, מַעֲשֵׂר names what was given to Melchizedek, and מִכֹּל specifies that the tenth came from everything. The gift to the priest supports the sense “tithe.”
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: a tenth given as a tithe

analysis.evidence: In מַעֲשֵׂר מִכֹּל, “a tenth of everything,” כֹּל stands independently and refers to everything from which the tenth was taken. The preposition marks the whole from which that share came.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מִן has its נ assimilated into כ, as the dagesh shows. כֹּל is a masculine singular noun in the absolute state.
